newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak interbank market cool to T-bill yield rise.
newsitem.headline: Slovak interbank market cool to T-bill yield rise.

text.p: Slovak money market rates are seen holding at current levels despite a recent rise in the yield of Finance Ministry T-bills, one of the key determining factors of local money rates, dealers said on Thursday.

They said that banks appeared to have their portfolios filled through to the end of the year, and may have little interest in non-taxed revenue from the ministry's T-bills, allowing rates to ease on a short-term liquidity surplus.

"The current T-bill yields are unbelievable, but we expect interbank money rates to stagnate at the present levels with banks' untaxed revenue balanced for the year," Daniel Bytcanek, a Polnobanka analyst, told Reuters.

Some said that only a few banks, mainly those posting losses including one of the market's largest players, were interested in untaxed T-bills, ideally at a rate equal to gross revenues such as deposits.
Slovak banks cover their costs with taxed revenue such as interbank deposits.

"Tax difference between T-bills and deposits has been eliminated, but anything from now on will be a tax-free revenue game, meaning a further increase in T-bills to over 12 percent," said ING Bank dealer Rastislav Zivor.
Average yield on the Finance Ministry's T-bills, hit 11.94 percent on Wednesday, up from 11.25 percent in the auction of similar bills last week, or from 9.3 percent a month ago.
Slovak interbank money rates held steady on Thursday, with overnights within a 12.0-12.7 percent offer range.

"The market is in a short-term surplus, but interest in untaxed revenue is not so significant, so why would banks not push the T-bill yields up when the chance is there?" said Jozef Bozek of Tatra Banka.

Looming on the horizon, analysts said, is the refinancing of the state budget deficit, which widened sharply to 13.4 billion crowns for the January-September period from 7.9 billion in the first eight months of 1996, while the full-year deficit projection is 26.95 billion crowns.
However, due to the sufficient market liquidity the central bank said it had no reason to hike its repo rates, currently standing at 9.7 and 7.2 percent respectively.
Both are also key price determining factor on the market.
"Unless the repo rates change, I see the interbank market stable within its current rate range, and T-bill yields firming," Vaclav Petrek, a dealer with the country's largest credit bank VUB, said.
The central bank has said that the current T-bill yields were high, but sufficient for successful state budget deficit refinancing though the market.
It added that its participation in helping finance the state budget was limited, and it would only do so to prevent interest rates from rising.
But added Bytcanek: "The Finance Ministry will have to look for sources other than commercial banks to cover its needs."
